project.description: A local, AI-first project orchestrator that provides a web interface for managing multi-project workflows with Claude Code as the execution engine. It covers the full project lifecycle: ideation, specification, kanban-based planning, automated code generation via Claude Code CLI, real-time agent monitoring, and release management.
project.spec:
# Arij

**Your AI-powered project manager that actually writes the code.**

## 1. Project overview

Arij is an MIT-licensed, local-first project orchestrator for planning, building, reviewing, and releasing software with AI coding agents. It combines a multi-project control desk, specification editor, ticket registry, chat workspace, agent monitoring, Git automation, QA reports, project memory, and release management in one Next.js application.

Claude Code is the default execution engine. Named agents can instead use OpenAI Codex, Oh My Pi, or Antigravity (`agy`). An OpenAI-compatible HTTP endpoint provides a direct, low-latency chat path; it is not a build, review, QA, or merge provider.

Arij has no hosted service, Arij account, cloud synchronization, or telemetry. Its database, documents, logs, clones, worktrees, and runtime artifacts remain on the local machine. Configured AI CLIs, OpenAI-compatible endpoints, Git remotes, and GitHub APIs may still communicate with their respective external services.

The package manifest reports version `0.1.0`. The only recorded product release and Git tag are `0.0.1` and `v0.0.1`; the main branch contains substantial completed work beyond that release.

### 1.1 Current implementation state

The GitHub import lifecycle is complete. Arij can attach a project to an existing local directory; import a GitHub repository from a supported URL or `owner/repo` shorthand; clone into an app-managed workspace and safely reuse a healthy matching clone; analyze a repository or short-circuit from an existing `arji.json`; populate GitHub ownership, clean remote URL, and detected default branch; and delete a clone only when database provenance, path containment, and an on-disk ownership marker all prove that Arij created it.

The current main branch also includes:

- Guarded epic and story transitions with explicit activity records for both accepted and refused moves.
- Manual and chat-driven epic creation, bug tickets, stories, dependencies, comments, screenshots, and review findings.
- A redesigned ticket detail overlay with a hierarchical sticky header, mobile-safe layout, and a compact activity feed.
- Isolated epic branches and Git worktrees for code-producing agents.
- Single-ticket pipelines, dependency-aware batch builds, night runs, Team Mode, and Full Auto Mode.
- Simplified named-agent creation based on a name and CLI, with optional model overrides and advanced role/runtime configuration.
- Agent reliability badges and opt-in reliability-based Full Auto dispatch.
- Manual and release-triggered specification rewrites.
- Per-session memory distillation and cross-session Dreaming.
- GitHub pull requests, issues, releases, push/pull status, and synchronization logs.
- Persisted session chunks, outcome classification, usage reporting, full failure notifications, and stalled-session detection.
- Project-scoped Server-Sent Events with polling fallback.
- An opt-in red-to-green regression gate for bug tickets.
- Structured review verdicts persisted by `submit_findings` and used as the authoritative input to the guarded transitions.
- Structured acceptance-criteria grading (opt-in, default off).
- Visual session artifacts through `attach_artifact`.
- Scheduled routines: night runs, Dreaming, GitHub issue synchronization, CI watch, and retention.
- Agent friction reports and agent-created bug tickets.
- Model economy: per-agent-type model mapping and an opt-in second opinion before Full Auto merge.
- Recurring-failure digests that cluster terminal outcomes, forensic reports, and critical findings.
- A deterministic verification stage running the project's configured `verify_commands` inside the epic worktree, persisted as `verify_reports`.
- A unified execution order where `position` is the single source of truth for board order and Full Auto dispatch.
- Board refinement passes over Backlog and To do.
- A persistent chat mode that keeps a warm CLI process per conversation.
- A token-volume estimate of the prompt a dispatch will send.
- Per-CLI named-agent options and a persona pre-prompt.
- The control desk in place of the Kanban board: `/` shows every project's work in attention strata, `/projects/:id` scopes the same desk to one project, `/tickets` is the exhaustive registry and the only table view, and `to_merge` marks work whose review passed and that awaits the merge.

### 1.2 Development boundary

Measured against `main` at 3183240e (2026-09-07). Work in flight on feature branches, not part of stable main-branch behavior:

- **E-BwEtdU8xBcbs**: composite agents — an ordered fallback list of named agents replacing the retired `escalates_to` escalation.
- **E-arij-155**: an English-only interface on a localization substrate.
- **E-arij-246**: a shared `dispatchBackgroundSession` helper and the decomposition of `runPipeline` / `dispatchPipelineStage` along stage boundaries.
- **B-arij-238**: a stranded `running` QA report keeps `/projects/:id/qa` polling every report body.
- **B-arij-210**: the React Compiler bails on 48 of 113 probeable components with no diagnostic.
- Narrow-viewport and accessibility fixes on the desk, the chat composer, the QA dialogs, and the Piscine primitives (B-arij-207, 208, 209, 215, 219, 220, 222, 223, 225, 245), one e2e parallelism race (B-arij-199), and B-arij-237 queued behind them.

Principal backlog items (the `/tickets` registry is the exhaustive list):

- **E-arij-135**: an `arjj` integration branch, with builds based on it and an `arjj` to default-branch pull request in the GitHub sync.
- **Runtime safety**: the server listens on all interfaces while the proxy trusts a spoofable `Host` header (B-arij-247); Claude Code cancellation cannot escalate to SIGKILL and never signals the process group (B-arij-250); `PRAGMA foreign_keys=OFF` inside rebuild migrations is a no-op under drizzle's transaction (B-arij-251); a rejected release of an unfinished ticket still creates the Git branch and tag (B-arij-239).
- **Delivery**: the CI test job never reaches `npm test` because `npm audit` exits first (B-arij-248); the regression gate copies `__tests__/helpers/*` onto the merge-base, so a helper fix can never show red (B-arij-260); the prompt-sweep VACUUM claim is spent on the first budgeted run (B-arij-254); nothing reconciles `qa_reports` at boot (B-arij-253) and a cancelled QA check leaves its report row unfinished (B-arij-258).
- **Documents and chat**: uploads above 11 MiB return 500 despite the 20 MiB route limit (B-arij-240) and stay stuck on Uploading after a network failure (B-arij-241); a failed conversations fetch reads as an empty project and creates a duplicate conversation (B-arij-259); the spec editor's document-mention popover is clipped by its card (B-arij-257).
- **UI hygiene**: the second-opinion prompt injects the full branch diff with no size budget (B-arij-163); six SelectPill controls carry an unbounded name (B-arij-255); the ticket overlay still walks the whole session list when the ticket has no session (B-arij-262); NamedAgentSelect reports an empty change inside a form (B-arij-261).

These items must not be described as current product behavior until they are merged.

## 2. Objectives

1. **Unify the software lifecycle.** Move from an idea or imported repository to a specification, actionable tickets, agent execution, review, merge, and release without switching project-management systems.
2. **Keep the application local-first.** Store project state, credentials, logs, documents, clones, worktrees, and runtime artifacts locally without an Arij account or hosted backend.
3. **Support multiple execution providers.** Claude Code as the built-in default, named agents backed by other supported CLIs, and a separate OpenAI-compatible direct-chat mode.
4. **Protect repositories during autonomous work.** Isolate code changes in worktrees, serialize conflicting work, honor the repository's real base branch, and refuse destructive filesystem actions without explicit ownership evidence.
5. **Make automation observable and interruptible.** Persist session state and output, classify terminal outcomes, surface failures and questions, expose live activity, support cancellation, and retain an audit trail.
6. **Automate without bypassing workflow rules.** Route manual actions, MCP requests, imports, pipelines, approval, release, and Full Auto through the same transition service.
7. **Preserve project context.** Inject the specification, learned memory, relevant tickets, user-authored comments, screenshots, and mentioned documents into the prompts that need them.
8. **Improve dispatch quality from evidence.** Show per-agent reliability and duration statistics and, optionally, select the strongest sufficiently sampled agent when the user has not chosen.
9. **Replace prose-only confidence with mechanical evidence.** Execute deterministic gates and persist structured verdicts, grading reports, and review artifacts so that agent assertions are never treated as proof.
10. **Make the cost of a dispatch legible before it is spent.** Where a provider meters an account by rolling window, show what remains at the moment the agent is chosen, rather than after the quota is exhausted.

## 3. Product principles and constraints

### 3.1 Local execution and access

- A single local Next.js application backed by SQLite.
- API access is restricted to localhost host/origin values by default; additional origins require explicit `ALLOWED_ORIGINS` configuration.
- No multi-user authentication, cloud synchronization, external queue, worker service, or event broker.
- Long-running agents are local child processes. Authentication and provider-specific configuration belong to their respective CLIs.
- Scheduler queues, launch closures, active pipeline registries, live night-run state, Full Auto runtime locks, MCP tokens, and SSE subscriptions live in the server process.
- Agent session rows, chunks, settings, documents, tickets, releases, and batch tags are durable.
- On restart: queued sessions whose launch closures were lost are cancelled as orphaned; running sessions are failed and any unverifiable mid-run review promotion is pulled back when possible; active pipelines and waves are not resumed; night-run summaries can be partially reconstructed from tagged session rows; Full Auto restarts from its persisted settings; scheduled routines resume from their persisted `last_run_at`.
- GitHub clone and repository analysis requests are synchronous and have no background cancellation service.

### 3.2 Database and migrations

- SQLite runs with WAL mode and foreign keys enabled. Drizzle migrations are applied at server startup.
- Migrations are **hand-written** under `lib/db/migrations/`. `npx drizzle-kit generate` must not be run: snapshot files stop at `0013` while the journal is far ahead, so generate would diff against stale state and emit wrong DDL.
- A relational change requires a numbered SQL migration, a new monotonically increasing entry in `meta/_journal.json`, and a `when` value greater than every previously applied migration.
- Numbered migration files collide between concurrent branches. Re-check the highest number and the journal tail against the current `main` tip immediately before merging, name the tip checked, and treat the reconciliation as expiring.
- A migration adding a UNIQUE or partial-unique index is only proven on a *clean* database. Validate against a copy of a real dev DB, not just a fresh one.
- Settings keys, document kinds, and session agent types are free-form text and need no migration unless the relational schema changes.
- Legacy databases without migration bookkeeping are baseline-stamped and then advanced through the runtime migration path.

### 3.3 Git and repository safety

- `simple-git` is the Git integration library; GitHub API operations use `@octokit/rest`; the `gh` CLI is not part of the architecture.
- GitHub imports are full clones. `--depth` and `--single-branch` are forbidden.
- Code-producing work runs in an epic-specific branch and worktree, never directly in the project's base checkout. Stories within one epic share the epic branch and are serialized.
- Worktrees live in the repository's sibling `.arij-worktrees` directory; worktrees outside it are treated as user-owned.
- The stored or repository-derived default branch is authoritative; `main` and `master` are fallbacks.
- Existing directories are never silently overwritten. A matching healthy clone may be fetched and reused; a mismatching or unowned destination is a conflict. Local repositories supplied by the user are never deleted.
- Clone deletion requires `projects.clone_source = "github"`, path containment inside the current projects root, and a valid `.git/arij-clone.json` marker.

### 3.4 Credentials and external communication

- The GitHub PAT is stored in the local `settings` table under `github_pat`; `GITHUB_TOKEN` is not read.
- Clone and reuse-fetch first try anonymously; authentication is retried only for credential-related failures. Authenticated Git uses a one-command `http.extraHeader`.
- Clone errors are redacted for authorization headers, URL user information, bearer tokens, GitHub token patterns, and the exact supplied secret.
- Credentials stored per project must be masked on the way out of the API, not only in the UI; test fixtures that serve the raw secret are part of the bug.
- Ordinary push, pull, and tag-push rely on the machine's Git credential configuration.
- OpenAI-compatible credentials are stored locally but sent to the configured endpoint when that chat mode is used.
- AI CLI providers may transmit prompts, code, and project context according to their own configuration and service terms.

### 3.5 Workflow integrity

- Epic and story status writes go through `lib/workflow/transition-service.ts` and the workflow engine. Successful moves are logged; guard refusals create explicit same-state activity entries.
- A build moves its target — and, for story work, the parent epic — to `in_progress` before its queued session row is created, and that session then owns the state.
- The sole owning code session may move its own target only from `in_progress` to `review`. It cannot demote, approve, complete, or move a story's parent epic directly.
- Successful epic builds move the epic and the stories in the build to `review`; successful story builds move the story, and the parent epic advances only when every sibling is in `review` or `done`.
- A negative review returns the affected scope to `in_progress`.
- `review -> done` requires an approval or merge source, a completed review where required, and no open blocking findings. The structured `submit_findings` verdict is the authoritative input; open `[critical]`/`[major]` findings block completion even under an approving verdict.
- `released` is terminal and may only be entered by the system during release creation.
- Agent sessions cannot approve their own work through ordinary status updates.
- `arji.json` imports reconcile content transactionally and route status changes through the same guards; refused statuses are reported and skipped.

### 3.6 Testing and delivery

- Unit, integration, and component tests live primarily in `__tests__/` and run with Vitest; browser tests live in `e2e/` and run with Playwright.
- Vitest excludes dependencies, build output, app-managed clones, `.claude` worktrees, and runtime data artifacts. Vitest filters do not run `.spec.ts` files — a regression proof needs a red `*.test.*`.
- CI uses Node.js 22 and runs the Vitest suite on pushes and pull requests. Step order decides what a job proves: an audit step placed before the test step makes the test step unreachable.
- Any CI step running `next build` must set `NODE_ENV` explicitly; sessions inherit `NODE_ENV=development` from the dev server and the build then dies on a bogus prerender error.
- Bug fixes are expected to include a regression test with a demonstrated failing state. The mechanical red-to-green gate can enforce this, but it copies `**/__tests__/**` onto the merge-base, so a fix living in a test helper can never show red under it.
- Playwright's own chromium download fails on this machine; drive the system Chrome with `channel: "chrome"`. `E2E_PORT` defaults to 3100 for every checkout — pick an explicit free port.
- Never `pkill` the running `next dev`: it is the live Arij orchestrator and killing it drops the in-memory MCP token for every live session.
- Claims that need a real browser (rendered text, computed formatting, focus-ring visibility, whether a badge wraps) are visual claims: say which were verified in a browser and which stayed source-only.

### 3.7 Design system (Piscine)

- `components/piscine/index.ts` is the shared vocabulary (`stratum` / `fill` / `tone` / `size`) and the single import surface. Tokens live in `app/globals.css` (`:root` = day, `.dark` = night); raw colour strings for SVG/canvas/`style` come from `lib/piscine/tokens.ts`. Never a hex.
- **Colour is the stratum you are on or the project identity (`projectTone`) — never state.** State is a word, an icon, or motion. This governs any status, quota, or health indicator: no green/amber/red gauge.
- Filled controls are `--action` (deep water-green), never black.
- `components/piscine/TopBar.tsx` is mounted once by `app/layout.tsx` and is the app's only chrome. A screen renders no page header of its own, and there is no left rail.
- No drag and drop anywhere. `@dnd-kit/*` remains in `package.json` but no source file imports it; re-ordering happens in the ticket overlay or Refinement.
- Piscine primitives that don't spread `...rest` silently swallow props — `data-testid` is the standing casualty, and TypeScript does not catch it. Assume the omission is the default in `components/piscine/`.
- A blanket `outline-none` kills a focus ring that a sibling `focus-visible:` class claims to draw; a class-presence assertion is not a visibility assertion.

## 4. Technical stack

| Technology | Role |
|---|---|
| Runtime | Node.js 20, 24 or newer |
| Application | Next.js 16.1 App Router, TypeScript 5.9 |
| UI | React 19.2, Tailwind CSS v4, shadcn/Radix components under the Piscine design system |
| Drag and drop | None |
| Database | SQLite through better-sqlite3, WAL mode, foreign keys enabled |
| ORM and validation | Drizzle ORM and Zod |
| Git | Git CLI through `simple-git` |
| GitHub | `@octokit/rest` |
| Agent execution | Local CLI child processes behind a common provider interface |
| Agent tool protocol | Model Context Protocol (`@modelcontextprotocol/sdk`) |
| Direct chat | OpenAI-compatible HTTP chat completions endpoint |
| Real-time UI | Server-Sent Events with reconnect and polling fallback |
| Markdown | `react-markdown` and `remark-gfm` |
| Documents | `mammoth` for DOCX and `pdf-parse` for PDF |
| IDs | `nanoid` |
| Tests | Vitest, Testing Library, jsdom, and Playwright |
| Packaging | npm package with the `arij` CLI wrapper |

## 5. Implemented product surface

### 5.1 Projects and repository import

A project can be created against an existing local directory or imported from GitHub. The import flow supports a validated local path; GitHub HTTPS, SSH-shaped, `git://`, or `owner/repo` shorthand with strict segment validation and clone-path containment; separate Cloning and Analyzing states; an editable preview; an `arji.json` short-circuit; automatic epic/story creation followed by an `arji.json` export; a deterministic clone destination; reuse of a healthy matching clone; replacement only of broken clone directories carrying Arij's marker; and provenance-guarded deletion. Imports normalize the remote to a clean HTTPS URL and populate `gitRemoteUrl`, `githubOwnerRepo`, and `defaultBranch`.

### 5.2 The control desk and the ticket registry

`/` is the cross-project control desk, organized as attention strata rather than columns: **Your turn** (questions, failures, merge conflicts), **Working**, **Ready to land**, and **Up next**. `/projects/:id` is the same desk scoped to one project. `/tickets` is the exhaustive registry and the only table view.

Ticket state still moves backlog → todo → in_progress → review → to_merge → done → released; those statuses are data, no longer drawn as columns. The surface provides feature epics and red bug tickets with readable IDs; user stories, descriptions, acceptance criteria, priorities, dependencies, and activity history; manual and API/MCP moves through the shared workflow engine; direct epic creation with inline stories; chat-driven refinement; bug creation with clipboard paste or file-picker screenshots; batch selection with parallel, sequential, and dependency-aware execution, and Team Mode; project-scoped SSE with polling fallback; a ticket detail overlay with a sticky header and compact chronological activity feed; and a friction register whose entries carry occurrence counts and triage state.

**Bug tickets** have a simplified creation flow — a direct form with no mandatory chat step — can optionally link to an epic, and support a "Create and Resolve" action that dispatches a selected agent through the existing build pipeline. When `bug_regression_check` is enabled, the branch must additionally carry a test green on the branch and red on the merge-base.

### 5.3 Chat, specifications, documents, and memory

The unified chat workspace provides tabbed conversations with persisted history, agent selection, attachments for supported CLI modes, and streamed responses. Regular conversations can use board tools to list and inspect tickets, create and edit them, request guarded status changes, post comments, inspect agent status, and start builds. Structured brainstorm and epic-creation conversations keep their output contracts isolated from board tools.

Project context can include the project name and description, the stored specification, learned memory, ticket and story details, user-authored comments and review findings, bug screenshots, and explicitly mentioned documents.

The specification can be edited manually, generated by an agent, or rewritten after a release when the opt-in setting is enabled; agent output replaces the saved specification only after a successful run with usable content, and successful writes re-export `arji.json`.

Documents support manual upload of PDF, DOCX, Markdown, plain text, and images; Markdown conversion; local storage and display of images; `@file` and `#file` references; repository scanning with user approval; idempotent case-insensitive duplicate handling; and per-file import failures without aborting the batch.

**Learned memory and Dreaming.** Each project has one capped Markdown memory document injected into relevant prompts. Per-session distillation can run manually; auto-distillation is off by default and skips failed, silent, or question-ending sessions. Dreaming is the cross-session pass: it reads at most 30 eligible terminal sessions from a rolling 14-day window bounded by the last successful cutoff, rewrites memory into four required sections, serializes against per-session distillation through one memory-writer lock, refuses to overwrite a manual edit made while it ran, and preserves one pre-Dreaming snapshot.

### 5.4 Named agents and sessions

The default creation path requires only a name and CLI, with availability indicators showing whether each CLI is detected and an optional model override. Advanced configuration exposes per-role prompts, global and project-scoped prompts, custom review agents, reviewer/provider segregation, runtime concurrency and watchdog settings, and reliability and duration statistics.

**Provider is a configuration concept.** A named agent owns its provider and model; outside the agent-configuration surfaces, the interface speaks in agents, not providers. Surfaces that still name a provider to the user are a known divergence being corrected.

A named agent is either `simple` — one provider and one model — or `composite`: an ordered list of simple agents held in `composite_agent_members`. A composite is a row of `named_agents` rather than a table of its own, so it is assignable anywhere a named agent already is. Nesting is refused at write time, so the list is flat and needs no cycle detection.

Agent resolution follows this precedence: explicit named-agent choice; project-scoped role assignment; global role assignment; built-in Claude Code fallback. Any step may resolve to a composite, which the resolver unfolds to one member — rank 0 by default, or the rank the retry ladder asks for. An exhausted rank is signalled explicitly rather than wrapping back to the first member. A composite emptied by member deletion is refused for an explicit choice and skipped (with a trace) for a background link of the chain.

Sessions record lifecycle status; provider, model, named-agent identity, and task type; project, epic, and story scope; prompt, CLI command display, branch, worktree, and logs path; ordered output chunks; terminal outcome and full error information; timestamps; token and reported-cost usage; batch or night-run attribution; and provider session identity where available. Sessions can be queued, monitored, cancelled, inspected, and resumed for providers whose CLI exposes usable continuity. A per-project in-process scheduler applies an optional concurrency cap — unlimited by default; positive values create a FIFO queue. Chat, specification generation, and merge resolution bypass the scheduler.

### 5.5 Automation modes

**Single-ticket autonomous pipeline.** `build -> [deterministic verification] -> [red-to-green regression gate, bug tickets only] -> [acceptance grading] -> review -> optional fix -> re-review`, with a per-stage retry ladder, a configurable fix-cycle limit, a hard limit of 12 sessions per run, cancellation/question/conflict/exhaustion policies, and a forensic diagnostic after exhausted attempts. A clean result leaves the ticket in Review; the pipeline never approves its own work.

The ladder is binary. A **simple agent** is retried as itself: attempt 1 uses the run's as-configured resolution, attempt 2 resumes the failed session when the machinery allows, later attempts start fresh on the same agent. No attempt switches agent, model, or provider. A **composite** runs the member at rank N-1 on attempt N, in `position` order; the length of the member list is the attempt budget for every stage it serves. What consumes a rank: a `failed`, `silent`, or `transition_refused` build. What does not: a negative review verdict, a failed regression gate, and a failed deterministic verification — those are fix cycles with their own budget. `asked_question` and `cancelled` stay terminal.

**Night runs** process selected epics through dependency-ordered waves with continue-or-stop failure policies, a consecutive-failure circuit breaker, a reported-cost cap, explicit stopping, notifications and morning summaries, and optional Dreaming afterwards.

**Full Auto Mode** is a standing per-project supervisor that reconciles in-flight state, merges eligible cleanly reviewed epics, dispatches reviews within the review budget, and dispatches builds within the build budget. It considers To Do and unoccupied In Progress work while skipping tickets that are busy, awaiting a reply, blocked, owned elsewhere, or parked. It provides separate budgets, explicit build and review agent choices, opt-in smart dispatch, activity entries for automatic choices and skips, a fresh-review requirement and blocking-finding checks before merge, an optional second opinion, deterministic verification of delivered code, soft parking after three consecutive failures, and hard parking after unresolved merge conflicts.

**Scheduled routines** are process-local and project-scoped: `night_run`, `dreaming`, `github_issue_sync`, `ci_watch`, and `retention`, one of each kind per project, with a daily `HH:MM` time and an enable flag. The scheduler claims a run by writing `last_run_at` before launching the action.

### 5.6 Reviews, QA, and releases

Built-in reviews cover security, code quality, compliance, feature completeness, and custom reviews. Findings are stored with file and line anchors and may be linked to the filing session; open findings block guarded completion. The overall verdict is the structured `submit_findings` verdict persisted on `agent_sessions.review_verdict`.

QA supports technology checks, E2E test sessions, custom prompts, named-agent selection, persisted reports and history, creating epics from findings, recurring-failure digests, and friction reports. QA checks are agent-driven; Arij executes `verify_commands`, the regression gate, and grading independently of the agents' assertions.

Release creation accepts completed unreleased epics, generates a changelog or falls back to ticket titles, creates or reuses a `<version>` branch, writes and commits `CHANGELOG.md`, tags the release commit, optionally pushes and creates a draft GitHub release, moves included epics to Released, and emits events and an optional webhook.

### 5.7 GitHub integration

Once `githubOwnerRepo` and a PAT are configured: detecting and connecting remotes, branch ahead/behind status, guarded push and pull with conflict reporting, issue synchronization and triage, label-to-type mapping, importing issues as tickets, creating draft pull requests, creating and publishing releases, and recording operations in `git_sync_log`.

### 5.8 Usage and remaining capacity

Arij persists per-session token and reported-cost usage and aggregates it on `/usage`. Providers that meter an account by rolling window (a 5-hour window, a weekly allowance) expose that remaining capacity at the point where an agent is chosen, so that a dispatch is not made blind against an exhausted account.

Remaining capacity is a property of the **credential scope** an agent's configuration resolves to, not of the named agent itself: two named agents backed by the same account share one window, and two agents on the same account therefore show the same figure. Storage is keyed by credential scope; the read API is keyed by named agent. The word *provider* does not appear in the resulting badge or in its public API.

An agent's capacity presentation is one of four states:

| State | Rendering | Origin |
|---|---|---|
| Windowed quota | `5 h · 38 % left`, `week · 61 % left` | measured, cached, with an explicit freshness |
| Direct API | `direct API` | derived from the agent's configuration |
| Local / unmetered | `∞` | derived from the agent's configuration |
| Indeterminate | `usage unknown` | measurement absent, failed, or stale |

Only the first state requires a collector, a TTL, and a cache; the other three are pure functions of the named agent's stored configuration. A missing measurement is never rendered as `0 %` and never as `100 %`.

## 6. Architecture

### 6.1 Runtime overview

`Browser <-> HTTP + SSE -> Next.js API routes <-> SQLite / Drizzle <-> in-process scheduler, watchdog, event bus, pipelines, routines, and supervisors <-> AI CLI child processes + OpenAI-compatible HTTP endpoints + Git CLI through simple-git + GitHub API through Octokit`

Arij is intentionally a single-process local application. The database is the durable state source; in-process registries coordinate active work but are not a durable job queue.

### 6.2 Filesystem layout

`data/arij.db`, `data/sessions/<session-id>/`, `data/documents/<project-id>/`, `data/uploads/<project-id>/`, `lib/db/migrations/`, and the managed `projects/<owner>-<repo>/` root with its sibling `.arij-worktrees`. Session artifacts are copied under `data/sessions/<session-id>/artifacts/`; the database stores only the generated basename, never an agent-controlled source path. The projects root defaults to `~/projects` and is overridable with the absolute `projects_root` setting.

### 6.3 Provider layer and MCP channel

`lib/providers/` defines a shared interface for spawning, streaming, selecting, resuming, and checking CLI availability. Availability is probed through `provider.isAvailable()` (a `which` by default). Shared child-process behavior includes bounded output handling, CLI session ID extraction, ordered chunk persistence, usage extraction, command display with prompt and secret redaction, and SIGTERM-to-SIGKILL cancellation.

Claude Code and Codex receive per-spawn MCP configuration. The agent toolset exposes `get_ticket`, `update_ticket_status`, `post_comment`, `report_friction`, `attach_artifact`, `create_bug`, `ask_question`, `submit_findings`, and `submit_grading`. Each token is short-lived and scoped to a session, project, epic, story, and agent type, and is revoked when the process ends. Providers without per-spawn MCP injection still receive structured prompt context but cannot use Arij's structured tools.

The regular chat toolset exposes `list_tickets`, `get_ticket`, `create_ticket`, `update_ticket`, `update_ticket_status`, `post_comment`, `get_agent_status`, and `start_build`. Chat tokens are rejected by the agent-only routes.

A prompt above the kernel's argv ceiling (~128 KiB) fails to spawn with `E2BIG`; the out-of-argv prompt transport covers claude, codex, oh-my-pi, and agy.

### 6.4 Usage collection and capacity resolution

Usage arrives on two independent channels and they must not be conflated:

1. **Per-session consumption** — tokens and reported cost extracted from a finished session's output, already collected for Claude Code and Codex, persisted on `agent_sessions`, and aggregated by `/usage`. This is a *record of spend*, not a *statement of remaining capacity*.
2. **Account-level window state** — whatever a CLI exposes about its rolling windows: used, limit, unit, and reset time. Its channel differs per CLI (session output, a credentials or config file, an HTTP endpoint, rate-limit response headers) and it may not exist at all.

Capacity is stored per credential scope in a dedicated table and read through a service that caches with a per-scope TTL. No capacity read is performed synchronously during a render: the agent picker fetches one aggregated payload for the whole list, never one request per row. A stale value is served *marked stale*; a read error degrades to the indeterminate state and never breaks the agent list.

The derived states (`direct API`, `∞`) are computed from the named agent's stored configuration — an endpoint that is local, a mode that is unmetered — and are never inferred from a hard-coded list of names.

### 6.5 Durable state, events, and observability

SQLite stores projects, epics, bugs, stories, dependencies, and activity; conversations, messages, attachments, documents, and project memory; agent sessions, ordered chunks, prompts, named agents, composite membership, and role assignments; review comments, grading reports, verify reports, and persisted review verdicts; usage windows per credential scope; QA reports, releases, pull requests, and GitHub issues; session artifacts; scheduled routines and their run state; friction reports; Git synchronization logs, notifications, read cursors, and provider usage snapshots; and free-form global and project-scoped settings.

A session dispatched by a composite records the member that actually ran in `agent_sessions.named_agent_id` and the dispatching composite in `agent_sessions.composite_agent_id`, so reliability statistics stay measured per real agent.

The server emits project-scoped SSE events for ticket, session, release, and routine changes; clients reconnect with exponential backoff and poll when disconnected. The watchdog checks running sessions against their last persisted output and creates one stalled notification per stall, but never kills an agent automatically.

## 7. Key decisions

| Decision | Rationale |
|---|---|
| Local, Next.js, and SQLite | Installation simplicity and project data under the user's control |
| Multiple CLIs | Store provider and model choices without duplicating every CLI's authentication and runtime settings |
| OpenAI-compatible HTTP as chat-only | Low-latency conversation without pretending a stateless endpoint is a build or review runner |
| Named agents separate identity from task role | Configure understandable agents once and assign them globally, per project, per role, or per dispatch |
| Provider is configuration, not UI vocabulary | The user chooses an agent; which CLI backs it is a detail of that agent's setup, and leaking it into every picker forces the user to hold two models at once |
| Explicit agent choices beat automation | A user's selection always wins over smart dispatch |
| Worktrees and branches per epic | Parallel work across epics with one integration unit for stories, review, and merge |
| Central transition service | Manual actions, API calls, MCP actions, imports, approval, release, pipelines, and Full Auto share the same guards and audit trail |
| A specific agent or a composite, with no third path | Agent fallback is either refused outright or an ordered list the user wrote |
| A composite is a row of `named_agents` | Every existing `named_agent_id` foreign key and both pickers keep working untouched |
| The session records both the composite and the member | Grouping runs by the dispatching list would destroy per-agent reliability, duration, and cost statistics |
| Capacity is keyed by credential scope, exposed by agent | Two agents on one account share one window; keying storage by agent would create N drifting copies of one pool and double-count it in any future quota-aware dispatch |
| Capacity is a badge, never a coloured gauge | Piscine reserves colour for stratum and project identity; state is a word, an icon, or motion |
| Unknown capacity is its own state | Rendering an unmeasured account as `0 %` or `100 %` is a confident lie in the one place the user is deciding where to spend |
| Capacity reads are cached and aggregated | A picker that opens a network call per row is slower than the decision it informs |
| Mechanical gates, structured verdicts, persisted artifacts | Agent prose is not a substitute for mechanically executed checks |
| Full Auto merge gating | Unattended merge paths carry explicit mechanical evidence before touching the base branch |

## 8. Current limitations and exclusions

- GitHub is the only supported clone host; SSH-key-based private cloning and monorepo subdirectory imports are not supported.
- Clone and analysis requests are synchronous with no background cancellation service.
- Scheduler queues, active pipelines, wave registries, runtime locks, MCP tokens, and live subscriptions do not survive a restart. Full Auto configuration survives; its in-flight and parking state does not.
- Arij is a single-user local application. Team Mode is limited to Claude Code. OpenAI-compatible mode is chat-only and rejects image attachments.
- Providers other than Claude Code and Codex do not receive per-session MCP tools; review decisions for them retain the prose fallback.
- Deterministic verification runs only when `verify_commands` is configured, only inside a managed epic worktree that still exists, and never in the repository checkout. The bug-ticket regression check stays opt-in and off by default.
- Full Auto has no fix-cycle ladder: a failing verification returns the ticket to In Progress and repair depends on the next sweep.
- No ticket surface renders a verify report yet.
- Retention prunes terminal session output and caps oversized prompts only; QA reports, grading and verify reports, artifacts, and sync logs are not pruned.
- Full Auto only dispatches To Do and In Progress work; Backlog tickets must be promoted first.
- Smart dispatch remains a separate automatic-choice path, not unified into the composite model.
- A composite orders agents and nothing else: no per-member concurrency cap, no per-member timeout, no conditional routing. The scheduler's concurrency limit is per project, not per named agent.
- **Remaining-capacity coverage is provider-dependent and partial by construction.** A CLI that exposes no account window has no windowed state to show, and the agent falls back to the indeterminate badge. Capacity is displayed only; nothing in the dispatch path, Full Auto, or smart dispatch reads it or avoids an exhausted agent.
- Capacity figures are cached snapshots with a freshness stamp, not live readings; a window can be consumed by another tool on the same account between two reads.

## 9. Implementation plan

The work below is ordered most foundational first. The capacity epics assume the composite-agent and provider-vocabulary work is either merged or explicitly sequenced ahead of the badge surface.

epics.title: Spike: what each CLI actually exposes about account quota
epics.description:
Every downstream story in the capacity work rests on one unknown: what each configurable CLI actually reports about an account's rolling windows. This is not an implementation detail — it decides whether the collector, the storage shape, and the badge are feasible at all, and for which agents.

The subject set is the CLIs Arij can back a named agent with (`claude`, `codex`, `oh-my-pi`, `agy`) plus the OpenAI-compatible direct-chat endpoint. `agy` is the newest and the least documented: previous sessions measured its process behaviour (inherited environment, bare model names, `--add-dir`) but nothing about its quota surface.

For each CLI, the spike must determine the read channel (session output, a credentials or config file on disk, an HTTP endpoint, rate-limit response headers), the fields available, the unit, the window length, whether a reset timestamp is exposed, how expensive and how fresh a read is, and what is honestly unavailable. It must also determine **what identifies the credential scope** — the account, profile, or endpoint that owns the window — since that is the storage key for the whole feature.

The deliverable is measurement, not code. It gates the collector, the storage model, and the badge, and the answer may legitimately be "this CLI exposes nothing", which is a result that shapes the design rather than a failure of the spike.

The write-up outlives this ticket and belongs in `docs/qa/` as a committed markdown report, not in the session transcript.

user_stories.title: As a developer, I want a measured inventory of each CLI's quota surface so that the storage model is designed against facts rather than assumptions
user_stories.description:
Probe `claude`, `codex`, `oh-my-pi`, `agy`, and the OpenAI-compatible endpoint for account-level window state. For each: what channel carries it, what fields it holds, what unit and window length it uses, whether a reset timestamp is present, how a read is performed, and what it costs.

Distinguish carefully between the two channels that already exist in the codebase's vocabulary: per-session consumption extracted from a finished run (already collected for some providers, and a record of spend) and account-level remaining capacity (a statement about a window). A CLI can expose the first and nothing of the second.

Run the probes against the real CLIs installed on this machine. Where a CLI is not installed or not authenticated, say so explicitly rather than inferring its behaviour from documentation.
user_stories.acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] Each of `claude`, `codex`, `oh-my-pi`, `agy` and the OpenAI-compatible endpoint has a row stating: read channel, fields, unit, window length, reset timestamp availability, read cost, and read freshness
- [ ] Per-session consumption and account-level window state are reported as two separate columns; a CLI exposing only the former is recorded as having no window state
- [ ] For each CLI, what is genuinely unavailable is stated explicitly rather than left blank
- [ ] Every claim is marked as measured against the real CLI, or as source-only/documentation-only, with no unmarked claims
- [ ] CLIs that are not installed or not authenticated on this machine are named as such, and their rows are not filled in from documentation
- [ ] The probe commands used are recorded verbatim so a later session can re-run them after a CLI upgrade

user_stories.title: As a developer, I want the credential scope identified for each CLI so that two agents on one account are known to share one window
user_stories.description:
Determine what identifies the account, profile, or endpoint that owns a quota window for each CLI: a config path, an account id or email, a base URL, an API key fingerprint, or nothing at all.

This is the storage key for the whole feature. Keying capacity by named agent would create one drifting copy of the same pool per agent and would double-count it in any future quota-aware dispatch. Keying it by credential scope makes two agents on one account show the same figure, which is the truthful outcome and precisely the information the user needs when hesitating between them.

The scope identifier must be derivable from an agent's stored configuration without a network call, and must never itself be a secret written into a table — a stable non-reversible fingerprint is acceptable where the raw value is a credential.
user_stories.acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] For each CLI, the credential-scope identifier is named, along with how it is derived from a named agent's stored configuration
- [ ] It is stated for each CLI whether two named agents with different models can share one scope, and whether one agent can span two scopes
- [ ] Any scope identifier derived from a secret (API key, token) is a non-reversible fingerprint, never the raw value, and this is stated explicitly
- [ ] A CLI with no derivable scope identifier is recorded as such, and the consequence (its agents can only reach the indeterminate state) is stated
- [ ] The proposed scope key is checked against the existing named-agent configuration columns to confirm it needs no new user-facing setting
- [ ] Whether the OpenAI-compatible endpoint's locality (and therefore the `∞` state) is derivable from its stored base URL is answered explicitly

user_stories.title: As a maintainer, I want the spike's findings committed as a QA report so that the measurements outlive the session that took them
user_stories.description:
Write the inventory and the credential-scope analysis to a committed markdown report under `docs/qa/`, and name the file in the handoff. Verification write-ups that a later story depends on cannot live in a transcript.

The report must state which claims were measured against a real CLI and which stayed source-only, and must record the CLI versions probed — a quota surface is exactly the kind of thing an upstream release changes without notice.

The report should close with a go/no-go per CLI: which ones can support a windowed badge, which ones fall back to the indeterminate state, and what that means for the scope of the collector story.
user_stories.acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] A markdown report exists under `docs/qa/` carrying both the per-CLI inventory and the credential-scope analysis
- [ ] The exact version of each CLI probed is recorded
- [ ] Each claim is marked measured or source-only; no claim is unmarked
- [ ] The report closes with an explicit go/no-go per CLI for windowed capacity
- [ ] The consequences for the collector's scope are stated: which CLIs it must handle and which are out of reach
- [ ] The report's filename is named in the handoff
- [ ] No credential, token, or API key value appears anywhere in the report

epics.title: Usage windows: storage model keyed by credential scope
epics.description:
Persist account-level remaining capacity in a dedicated table keyed by credential scope, and derive an agent's capacity *classification* from its stored configuration.

The central design constraint, settled in discussion: storage is keyed by credential scope, the read API is keyed by named agent. Two named agents backed by the same account resolve to the same row and show the same figure. This keeps a single pool represented once, and it is what makes a later quota-aware dispatch able to count correctly.

The table holds the measurement: scope, window (`5h` / `week`), used, limit, unit, `resets_at`, `measured_at`, and source. The classification (`quota` / `direct_api` / `unmetered`) is *not* stored — it is a pure function of the named agent's configuration, so a local endpoint reads as unmetered without ever needing a measurement, and adding a new CLI does not require a data backfill.

The hard invariant: **an absent measurement is distinguishable from a measured zero.** An `agy` agent with no reported window must not render as `100 % left` and must not render as exhausted. This is the difference between an honest indicator and a confident lie at the exact moment the user is deciding where to spend.

Migrations here are hand-written: a numbered SQL file plus a `meta/_journal.json` entry whose index and `when` both increase. `npx drizzle-kit generate` must not be run. Because several branches add "the next" number concurrently, the highest number must be re-checked against the current `main` tip immediately before merge.

user_stories.title: As a developer, I want a `usage_windows` table keyed by credential scope so that one account's quota is stored exactly once
user_stories.description:
Add a table holding one row per (credential scope, window): scope key, window (`5h` / `week`), used, limit, unit, `resets_at`, `measured_at`, and source. Update `lib/db/schema.ts` alongside the migration — the schema file and the SQL are two copies of one contract and drift silently when only one is touched.

No foreign key to `named_agents`: the row belongs to an account, not to an agent, and it must survive an agent being renamed, reconfigured, or deleted. The scope key is opaque to the table.

Write the migration by hand as a numbered `.sql` file with a matching journal entry. Validate it against a copy of a real dev database, not only a fresh one — a uniqueness constraint is only proven where duplicate rows can already exist.
user_stories.acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] `usage_windows` exists with scope key, window, used, limit, unit, `resets_at`, `measured_at`, and source columns
- [ ] A unique constraint on (scope key, window) prevents two rows describing the same window
- [ ] The table has no foreign key to `named_agents`, and a row survives the deletion of every agent that resolved to it
- [ ] `lib/db/schema.ts` is updated in the same change and matches the SQL column-for-column
- [ ] The migration is a hand-written numbered file with a `meta/_journal.json` entry whose index and `when` both strictly increase; `npx drizzle-kit generate` was not run
- [ ] The migration applies cleanly on a fresh database and on a copy of `data/arij.db`, and both runs are reported
- [ ] The migration number is re-checked against the current `main` tip immediately before merge, and the tip checked is named in the handoff

user_stories.title: As a developer, I want an absent measurement to be distinct from a measured zero so that an unmeasured agent is never rendered as full or as empty
user_stories.description:
Make the indeterminate state a first-class value throughout the model, not an absence that a consumer coerces. A missing row, a row whose `limit` is unknown, and a row too stale to trust must all resolve to the same explicit indeterminate result, distinguishable from a row that genuinely reports zero remaining.

This has to hold at the type level, not by convention: a reader that can accidentally treat "no data" as `0` or as `100` will eventually do so, and the failure is silent and user-facing. The resolver's return type should make the three cases — measured value, explicitly unmetered, unknown — impossible to conflate.

Staleness is part of this: a value read long enough ago that its window may have reset is not a measurement any more, and the threshold must be a named constant rather than a literal scattered across call sites.
user_stories.acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] The resolver's return type distinguishes a measured window, an explicitly unmetered agent, and an unknown state, and a consumer cannot silently coerce one into another
- [ ] A credential scope with no row resolves to unknown, not to `0` and not to `100`
- [ ] A row whose `limit` is absent resolves to unknown even when `used` is present
- [ ] A row older than the staleness threshold resolves to stale-with-value, carrying both the value and its `measured_at`, never to a bare fresh value
- [ ] The staleness threshold is a named constant, defined once
- [ ] A row reporting genuinely zero remaining resolves to a measured zero and is distinguishable from unknown
- [ ] Unit tests cover all six cases above by asserting on the resolved variant, not on a rendered string

user_stories.title: As a developer, I want an agent's capacity class derived from its configuration so that local and direct-API agents need no measurement at all
user_stories.description:
Classify a named agent as `quota`, `direct_api`, or `unmetered` from its stored configuration. Only `quota` requires a measurement; the other two are pure functions and are correct the moment an agent is created.

Derive locality from a property — a loopback or private-network base URL, an endpoint with no credential — rather than from a hard-coded list of names, so that a user's own local endpoint is recognised without a code change. Same for direct API: it follows from the agent being backed by the OpenAI-compatible mode, not from its name.

This classification is `lib/`-internal and speaks in terms of provider configuration; it is exactly the layer where the word *provider* is allowed to live. What it returns to the UI is an agent-level classification with no provider vocabulary in it.
user_stories.acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] A pure function maps a named agent's stored configuration to `quota`, `direct_api`, or `unmetered` with no database read and no network call
- [ ] Locality is derived from the endpoint's address family or credential-absence, not from a hard-coded list of endpoint names
- [ ] An agent backed by the OpenAI-compatible mode against a remote endpoint classifies as `direct_api`
- [ ] An agent pointed at a loopback or private-network endpoint classifies as `unmetered`
- [ ] A CLI-backed agent classifies as `quota`, even when no measurement exists for its scope — it then resolves to unknown, not to unmetered
- [ ] The classifier's output type carries no provider name, and the value returned to the UI layer is agent-scoped
- [ ] Unit tests cover each class plus the boundary case of a CLI-backed agent with no measurement

epics.title: Antigravity (agy) usage collection
epics.description:
Extend usage collection to the `agy` provider, which today runs without contributing to any usage record. Claude Code and Codex already have per-session extraction; `agy` sessions terminate with no tokens, no reported cost, and no window state, so `/usage` under-reports and no capacity badge can exist for an `agy`-backed agent.

Two distinct deliverables, and the second is conditional on the spike: per-session consumption written to the session row like its siblings, and account-level window state written to `usage_windows` if and only if the spike found a channel that exposes it. If the spike found none, this epic delivers the first half and records the second as unreachable — which is an honest result, not a shortfall.

The standing trap in this area: a run that reports nothing must be journalled as *not reported*, never persisted as `0`. A zero in a usage column is a measurement, and writing one for an absent reading corrupts the aggregate on `/usage` and the badge at the same time.

Because `agy` inherits the environment of the process that spawned it and takes bare model names, any collection path must be exercised against a real `agy` invocation, not only against a stub. Stub-binary tests prove Arij's side of the boundary; they prove nothing about what the CLI actually emits.

user_stories.title: As a user, I want `agy` sessions to record their token and cost usage so that the usage page stops silently under-reporting
user_stories.description:
Extract per-session consumption from a finished `agy` run and persist it on the session row, following the existing extraction shape used for Claude Code and Codex rather than inventing a parallel path.

The extraction must tolerate the CLI's real output: partial output from a cancelled run, output interleaved with the agent's prose, and a run that emits no usage line at all. The last case is the important one — it is journalled as unreported and the columns are left null.

Verify against a real `agy` invocation. A stub binary can prove that Arij parses a known string; only a real run proves the string is the one `agy` emits.
user_stories.acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] A completed `agy` session persists token counts and reported cost on its session row when the CLI emits them
- [ ] A session whose output carries no usage information leaves the columns null and writes an explicit "usage not reported" trace — no `0` is persisted
- [ ] A cancelled or truncated `agy` session does not persist a partial figure as if it were final
- [ ] The extraction reuses the existing per-provider usage-extraction seam rather than adding a parallel code path
- [ ] `/usage` includes `agy` sessions in its aggregates, and the observed before/after figures on a seeded database are reported
- [ ] At least one assertion is made against output captured from a real `agy` run, and the handoff states which claims came from a real run and which from a stub

user_stories.title: As a user, I want `agy`'s account window state collected when the CLI exposes it so that an agy-backed agent can show remaining capacity
user_stories.description:
If the spike found a channel carrying `agy`'s account-level window state, collect it and write it to `usage_windows` under the credential scope resolved for the agent. If the spike found no such channel, this story delivers nothing and records the finding — `agy` agents then resolve to the indeterminate badge, which the design already accommodates.

Collection must be safe to run repeatedly and must not be on the request path of a render. Whatever channel it uses, a failure to read is a degradation to unknown, never an error surfaced to the user and never a partially written row.

Where the reading is derived rather than reported — inferring a window from accumulated session usage, for instance — say so in the `source` column, because a derived figure and a reported one deserve different trust and the badge's freshness marker depends on knowing which it has.
user_stories.acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] When `agy` exposes window state, a successful read writes one `usage_windows` row per window under the resolved credential scope, with `measured_at` and `source` populated
- [ ] A read failure leaves the previous row untouched and resolves to unknown or stale-with-value; no partial row is written and no error reaches the user
- [ ] Repeated collection is idempotent: it updates the existing row for a (scope, window) pair rather than accumulating rows
- [ ] A derived rather than directly reported figure is marked as such in `source`
- [ ] If the spike found no channel, the story is closed with that finding recorded in the QA report and `agy` agents are confirmed to resolve to the indeterminate state without error
- [ ] Collection never runs synchronously inside a request that renders the agent picker
- [ ] The handoff states whether the collection was exercised against a real authenticated `agy` account or only against a stub

epics.title: Capacity read service, cache, and aggregated API
epics.description:
Serve remaining capacity to the interface without making the agent picker wait on a CLI, a file read, or a network round trip.

Three constraints shape this. The picker must open at its current speed, so no capacity read may happen synchronously during a render. The list must cost one request, not one per row, so the route is aggregated over every named agent. And a read failure must degrade, never propagate — an agent list that fails to render because a quota probe timed out is strictly worse than one that shows `usage unknown`.

The cache is keyed by credential scope with a per-scope TTL, since read cost differs sharply between a config file and an HTTP endpoint. A value past its TTL but still present is served *marked stale* together with its `measured_at`: a figure from twenty minutes ago is useful information as long as it is labelled, and hiding it in favour of `unknown` throws away the only signal available.

The route's public shape is keyed by named agent id, and it carries no provider vocabulary. That is a deliberate contract: the storage layer thinks in credential scopes and providers, the API speaks agents. It also means the response naturally shows the same window figure against two agents sharing one account, which is correct and is exactly what the user needs to see when choosing between them.

user_stories.title: As a developer, I want a capacity service with a per-scope TTL cache so that the picker never waits on a quota read
user_stories.description:
Build the read service over `usage_windows` and the configuration-derived classifier. It resolves a named agent to a capacity state, caching per credential scope with a TTL chosen per scope kind — a local config file and a rate-limited HTTP endpoint do not deserve the same interval.

Refresh happens outside the render path. A cache miss returns unknown immediately and schedules a refresh rather than blocking; the next read benefits. This is the difference between an indicator that costs nothing and one that makes the user wait to learn how much quota they have.

A stale entry is served with its value and its `measured_at`, flagged stale. Only a genuinely absent measurement resolves to unknown.
user_stories.acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] The service resolves a named agent id to one of: measured window, stale window with `measured_at`, direct API, unmetered, or unknown
- [ ] Cache entries are keyed by credential scope, so two agents sharing an account share one entry and one refresh
- [ ] TTL is configurable per scope kind and defined as named constants, not literals at call sites
- [ ] A cache miss returns immediately with unknown and schedules a refresh; it never blocks the caller on a CLI or network read
- [ ] An expired-but-present entry is served marked stale with its value and `measured_at`, not discarded
- [ ] A refresh failure leaves the previous value in place and is traced; it never throws to the caller
- [ ] Unit tests cover hit, miss, expiry, refresh failure, and two-agents-one-scope sharing

user_stories.title: As a developer, I want one aggregated capacity endpoint keyed by agent so that rendering a list of agents costs a single request
user_stories.description:
Expose `GET /api/usage/agents` returning capacity state for every named agent in one payload, keyed by named agent id. One request for the whole picker, never one per row — a per-row fetch pattern is a known recurring defect class in this codebase and it must not be reintroduced here.

The response carries only what the badge renders: the capacity state, the window and figures where they exist, `resets_at`, and a freshness marker. It must not ship provider names, endpoint URLs, credential fingerprints, or the raw scope key — the scope key is internal, and a client that received it could correlate accounts across agents in ways the UI has no need for.

Validate and fail cleanly: an unknown agent id is a typed 4xx, never a 500, and a partial failure across scopes still returns the agents that resolved.
user_stories.acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] `GET /api/usage/agents` returns capacity for all named agents in one response, keyed by named agent id
- [ ] Rendering the full agent picker issues exactly one capacity request, verified by counting requests under `next start` rather than `next dev` (Strict Mode double-invokes effects in dev)
- [ ] The payload contains no provider name, endpoint URL, credential fingerprint, or raw scope key
- [ ] Two agents sharing one credential scope return identical window figures
- [ ] A failure to read one scope still returns every other agent's state, with the failed one resolving to unknown
- [ ] The route responds in well under the picker's open latency with a cold cache, and the measured figure is reported
- [ ] A route-level test asserts the response shape, including the absence of the forbidden keys, so a later widening of the query cannot silently reintroduce them

epics.title: Remaining-capacity badge in the agent selector
epics.description:
Show remaining capacity where the decision is actually made: in the agent picker, at the moment an agent is chosen for a dispatch.

Four states, three of which need no measurement at all. A windowed quota renders as a figure and its window (`5 h · 38 % left`, `week · 61 % left`); a direct-API agent renders `direct API`; a local or unmetered agent renders `∞`; and anything unmeasured, failed, or stale renders `usage unknown` — never `0 %`, never `100 %`.

Two design constraints are non-negotiable. **No colour encodes state**: Piscine reserves colour for the stratum and the project identity, so a nearly-exhausted quota is signalled by its number and, if needed, a word or an icon — not by turning amber. **No provider vocabulary reaches the badge**: the user picked an agent, and which CLI backs it is configuration.

There is a sequencing point worth stating plainly: the epic that removes provider vocabulary from the pickers should land before this badge, or the badge is inserted into a surface that still names providers and has to be reworked. If that epic is not ready, this one still ships — the badge simply must not add any new provider mention of its own.

The picker is a Piscine surface, which brings its standing hazards: primitives that swallow `data-testid` without a type error, focus rings defeated by a blanket `outline-none`, controls that flip uncontrolled-to-controlled when their fetched data lands, and a badge whose text length can push a long agent name into overflow at narrow widths. Each needs checking in a real browser rather than in the diff.

user_stories.title: As a user choosing an agent, I want its remaining capacity shown beside its name so that I do not dispatch against an exhausted account
user_stories.description:
Render the capacity badge in the shared agent selector, fed by the aggregated endpoint. The badge reads as a compact phrase: the window and what remains for a metered agent, `direct API` for a direct-API agent, `∞` for a local one, `usage unknown` otherwise.

A stale value is shown with its age rather than hidden — a figure from twenty minutes ago beats no figure, provided it says so. Where a window has a known reset, the reset time is available on the badge, since "12 % left, resets in 40 min" and "12 % left, resets Tuesday" are entirely different decisions.

The selector must not slow down: it renders immediately with whatever the aggregated payload holds, and capacity arriving late must not shift the layout under the pointer or change what a click selects.
user_stories.acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] All four states render in the picker: windowed quota, `direct API`, `∞`, and `usage unknown`
- [ ] An unmeasured agent renders `usage unknown` and never `0 %` or `100 %`
- [ ] A stale value renders with its age; a fresh value renders without one
- [ ] `resets_at` is surfaced for a windowed agent when known
- [ ] The picker opens with no measurable delay compared to before the badge, and capacity arriving after first paint does not shift rows or change the hit target
- [ ] Two agents on one account show the same figure, and this is verified in a running app rather than only in a unit test
- [ ] Each state is verified in a real browser and the screens checked are named in the handoff

user_stories.title: As a user, I want the badge to obey the Piscine rules so that capacity reads as information rather than as an alarm
user_stories.description:
Compose the badge from `@/components/piscine` with tokens from `app/globals.css` and `lib/piscine/tokens.ts`. No hex. And, specifically: **no colour carries state**. A depleted quota is not a red badge; it is a number, and at most a word or an icon. Colour in Piscine means the stratum you are on or the project you are looking at, and a quota gauge that repurposes it breaks the one rule the system is built on.

A neutral progress bar on a fill token is acceptable if it helps scanning, provided its colour does not vary with the value.

The standing Piscine hazards apply. Check that `data-testid` actually reaches the DOM — the primitives silently swallow unspread props and TypeScript will not tell you. Check the focus ring paints, in both day and night, in a real browser: a class-presence assertion proves the token is written, not that it is visible. And check the badge does not push a long agent name into horizontal overflow at 390 px, where the desk's collapsed chat rail leaves roughly 44 px less width than `/`.
user_stories.acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] The badge is composed from `@/components/piscine` primitives; no new lookalike is introduced and the barrel was checked first
- [ ] No colour varies with the capacity value; a low quota and a high one differ by their text, not their hue
- [ ] Every colour comes from a token; no hex string appears in the diff
- [ ] Any progress bar uses a fixed fill token independent of the value
- [ ] `data-testid` is confirmed present in the rendered DOM, not merely passed as a prop
- [ ] The focus ring on every interactive element in the picker is confirmed visible in a real browser in both day and night themes
- [ ] At 390 px, a long agent name plus badge produces no horizontal overflow of `documentElement`; the widths measured are named, and the band above the breakpoint is either measured or explicitly left to its own ticket
- [ ] The selector renders a defined value from first paint and does not flip uncontrolled-to-controlled when the agent list or the capacity payload resolves

user_stories.title: As a user, I want the badge to speak about agents rather than providers so that the interface keeps one vocabulary
user_stories.description:
The badge, its tooltip, its accessible names, and the endpoint that feeds it must contain no CLI or provider name. The user chose an agent; which binary backs it belongs to that agent's configuration screen.

This matters beyond tidiness. The capacity figure is a property of an account shared across agents, and naming the CLI invites the reading that the quota belongs to the CLI rather than to the credential behind it — which is the exact misconception the credential-scope storage model exists to prevent.

If the epic removing provider vocabulary from the pickers has not landed, this story does not fix the surrounding picker; it only guarantees the badge adds no new mention. Say which of the two situations applied.
user_stories.acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] No provider or CLI name appears in the badge text, its tooltip, or its accessible name
- [ ] The capacity payload consumed by the badge carries no provider field
- [ ] Terms describing capacity are agent-scoped throughout the user-facing copy
- [ ] A test asserts the rendered badge contains none of the known provider identifiers, so a later change cannot reintroduce one silently
- [ ] The handoff states whether the provider-vocabulary epic had landed, and if not, confirms the badge added no new provider mention to the picker
- [ ] The `lib/` layer keeps its provider vocabulary; the boundary where it stops is named in the handoff

epics.title: Capacity detail on the usage page
epics.description:
Give the badge's compressed figure a place to be read in full. `/usage` already aggregates per-session token and cost usage; this adds the account-window view beside it.

The two are genuinely different measurements and the page must not blur them. Per-session usage is a record of what was spent and it accumulates; a window is a statement about what remains and it resets. Presenting them as one number would be wrong in both directions.

Without cost display in scope — the user's call, and a real simplification — this surface is thin: windows, what remains in each, when each resets, where the figure came from, and how old it is. Provenance and freshness matter more here than in the picker, because this is where a user goes when the badge said something they doubt.

An agent whose account exposes nothing must read as unmeasured, with the reason available. "We cannot see this account's quota" and "this account has no quota" are different statements and the page must be able to tell them apart.

user_stories.title: As a user, I want a capacity section on the usage page so that I can see every account's windows, resets, and freshness in one place
user_stories.description:
Add a capacity band to `/usage` listing each credential scope's windows with what remains, `resets_at`, source, and `measured_at`. Group by scope so that agents sharing an account appear together under one window rather than as duplicated rows — the grouping is the clearest way to convey that they share a pool.

Keep account-window state visually and semantically separate from the existing per-session consumption aggregates. Label them so the distinction is legible without prior knowledge of the data model.

An unmeasured scope appears with its reason rather than being omitted; omitting it would make an unreadable account indistinguishable from an absent one.
user_stories.acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] `/usage` shows a capacity section listing each scope's windows with remaining, `resets_at`, source, and `measured_at`
- [ ] Agents sharing a credential scope are grouped under one window entry rather than duplicated
- [ ] Account-window state is visually and textually distinct from per-session consumption aggregates, and the labelling makes the difference legible
- [ ] An unmeasured scope is listed with its reason, not hidden
- [ ] A stale figure carries its age; a fresh one does not
- [ ] The section is composed from `StrataBand` and Piscine primitives, draws no page header of its own, and encodes no state in colour
- [ ] The page is verified in a real browser at 390 px and at desktop width with at least one scope in each state

user_stories.title: As a user, I want to distinguish an unreadable account from an unmetered one so that a blank figure is never mistaken for an unlimited one
user_stories.description:
Make the page say which of three situations holds: the account is unmetered by nature (a local endpoint), the account is metered but Arij cannot read its window, or the account is metered and the reading is simply old.

These collapse into one blank in a naive rendering, and the collapse is harmful in the direction that matters — a user reading a blank as "unlimited" will dispatch into an exhausted account. The distinction already exists in the data model as three separate resolved variants; this story is about not losing it at the last step.

Where a read is failing repeatedly, the page should say so plainly enough that the user can act on it — a misconfigured or expired credential is a real cause and it is fixable, but only if it is visible.
user_stories.acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] Unmetered, unreadable, and stale render as three distinguishable states, never as one blank
- [ ] An unmetered scope's `∞` is presented as a property of the endpoint, not as a measurement
- [ ] An unreadable scope names the reason at the granularity available (no channel, read failed, not authenticated)
- [ ] A repeatedly failing read is visible as such rather than as a permanently stale value
- [ ] The copy avoids implying capacity where none was measured; the wording is verified by reading the rendered page, not the source
- [ ] A test covers all three states resolving to distinct rendered output
- [ ] Any provider identifier needed to explain a failure stays in `lib/` traces and does not surface in the page copy

epics.title: Branche d'intégration `arjj` : socle git main→arjj + PR `arjj`→défaut dans GitHub sync
epics.description:
## Contexte

Aujourd'hui le socle git d'Arij est la **branche par défaut** du dépôt (§3.3, §5.7) : les branches/worktrees d'épic partent de là, le merge (manuel + Full Auto) y retombe, et les releases `release/vX` + tag `vX` en découlent.

**Changement radical proposé :** Arij adopte sa propre branche longue-vie **`arjj`** comme tronc de travail. La branche par défaut (`main`/défaut) reste la **vérité amont** ; `arjj` est le **tronc Arij** où tout est intégré, et on shippe vers l'amont via une **PR `arjj` → défaut** proposée depuis l'écran GitHub sync (§5.8).

### Modèle cible

```text
main / défaut   (amont — source de vérité, inchangée §3.3)
  ^  PR `arjj` → défaut   (proposée dans GitHub sync, draft par défaut)
  |  sync guardé défaut → arjj   (pour rester mergeable)
arjj            (tronc Arij — longue-vie, Arij-owned)
  |  les branches épic forkent d'arjj ; le merge retombe sur arjj
  +-- epic-xxx (worktree isolé par epic, stories partagées)
```

### Conséquences (câblées dans les stories)
- Base des worktrees/branches d'épic → `arjj` (fallback défaut si mode off).
- Cible de merge (manuel + Full Auto) → `arjj` ; gardes de workflow inchangées, autre cible.
- Releases `release/vX` + tag `vX` découlent de `arjj`.
- Nouvelle action GitHub sync : **proposer une PR `arjj` → défaut** (Octokit, trackée, journalisée).
- Sécurité : `arjj` est un **artifact Arij** — jamais de force-push, jamais de suppression de la branche par défaut, preuve de provenance explicite (discipline du marqueur de clone §3.3).
- **Amendement du spec** : §3.3 (la branche par défaut reste l'amont ; `arjj` devient le tronc d'intégration Arij) et §5.7 (cibles de merge et de release) seront mis à jour avec l'implé.

### Décisions à trancher (à confirmer avant implé)
1. **Nom exact** de la branche (`arjj` par défaut, configurable par projet ?) — *spelling à valider*.
2. **Bascule dure ou opt-in** par projet (toggle `git_use_integration_branch`) ; défaut sur les nouveaux projets ?
3. PR `arjj` → défaut : **draft par défaut** (non destructif) ou régulière ?
4. Les **releases découlent de `arjj`** (vs de la PR mergée) — à valider.
5. Le **sync amont→`arjj`** est-il une op à la demande seulement, ou automatique avant chaque PR ?

user_stories.title: Socle : réglages + bootstrap de la branche d'intégration
user_stories.description: Ajouter `git_integration_branch` (défaut `arjj`) et `git_use_integration_branch` (bool) en settings (free-form, pas de migration). Au premier dispatch sur un projet avec le mode actif, créer `arjj` depuis la branche par défaut du dépôt et le mémoriser ; idempotent. `main`/défaut restent la vérité amont (§3.3 inchangée).
user_stories.acceptance_criteria:
- Les 2 clés se round-trip via l'API de settings.
- `arjj` est créée une seule fois depuis la branche par défaut, idempotent (pas de re-branche si elle existe).
- Si le toggle est off, comportement = aujourd'hui (base = défaut).
- Aucune écriture destructrice sur la branche par défaut.

user_stories.title: Worktrees/branches + merge retargetés sur `arjj`
user_stories.description: La création de branche/worktree d'épic part de `arjj` (fallback défaut si mode off/absent). Le merge manuel et Full Auto (épiques clean reviewés) retombent sur `arjj`.
